about: Two woods used to model the plates of stringed instruments, with the four plate stiffnesses that make wood orthotropic: D1 along the grain, D2 across it, D3 the twisting stiffness and D4 the coupling term. Every other solid this library holds is treated as isotropic, with one modulus and one Poisson ratio, which cannot say that spruce is sixteen times stiffer along the grain than across it. The table is printed after Woodhouse, whom it credits, and every row carries that attribution. The page prints the table with the woods as its columns and the properties as its rows, and this file turns it so that a wood is a row, which is how every other catalogue here is keyed. The page prints the stiffnesses in megapascals and they are held in pascals. Two of the maple cells carry an asterisk the footnote calls an intelligent guess, and they are marked as estimates rather than measurements.

rows.name: Maple
rows.note: Two of this row's four plate stiffnesses carry the table's asterisk: the table marks this cell with an asterisk and its own footnote calls the asterisked values “intelligent guesses in the absence of experimental data”, so it is the author's estimate and not a measurement. They are served, because the page prints them as numbers, but they are marked as estimates so that a caller who wants measurements can tell them apart. The relative scaling factor the page prints for maple, 1.4, does not follow from this row: the same row prints the relation as the fourth root of D1 over D3, and maple's D1 of 860 MPa and D3 of 170 MPa, neither of them asterisked, give 1.50. Spruce's 1.9 does follow from its own row. The factor is served as printed and the defect is registered in docs/ERRATA.md under “Rossing (2014), Table 15.5”.
